description: Looking for young innovators aged 13–18 to join our NASA Space Apps Challenge team! Our project focuses on developing a health monitoring system for astronauts, combining medical science, engineering, and technology. We welcome members with skills or interests in programming, coding, biomedical sciences, engineering, UI/UX design, and data analysis. Passion, creativity, teamwork, and a willingness to learn are essential!
summary:
ASTRA (Astronaut Health Monitoring & Decision-Support System) is a proposed software solution designed to help astronauts monitor and understand changes in their health during long-duration space missions.

The application brings five health-monitoring areas into one integrated interface: skeletal health, cardiovascular health, behavioral and mental wellbeing, radiation exposure, and general physiological health. It is designed to organise measurements from relevant monitoring devices, compare them with each astronaut's personal baseline, track changes over time, and present understandable status indicators such as STABLE, WATCH, and REVIEW.

ASTRA also aims to provide research-informed explanations and visual health trends, helping astronauts recognise noteworthy changes and communicate relevant information to medical teams. Its design considers the challenges of space missions, including limited connectivity and the need for accessible health information.

By combining multiple monitoring areas into one organised platform, ASTRA aims to make astronaut health information easier to understand and act upon. It is a decision-support concept, not a medical diagnostic system, and its proposed monitoring methods require further testing and validation.
details: ASTRA is a web-based astronaut health monitoring and decision-support system for the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions." What it does: ASTRA brings five NASA-identified spaceflight risk areas into one dashboard: bone and skeletal health, cardiovascular function, cognitive and behavioral well-being, radiation exposure, and physiology (blood pressure, glucose, sleep). Each astronaut is compared against their own baseline from early in the mission, using control-chart z-scores. Published clinical limits act as safety guards, for example the ISCD bone-density change threshold, blood pressure and glucose limits, and the NASA-STD-3001 radiation career limit. Each metric is shown as STABLE, WATCH or REVIEW, and each alert comes with a suggested action. How it works: Data can be entered manually, imported from CSV, or taken from a built-in simulated mission. It includes a reaction-time (PVT-style) cognitive test and a Reports page that exports CSV/JSON and a plain-text downlink packet for low-bandwidth communication with Earth. Everything runs in the browser with no server, so it keeps working during communication delays or outages. Benefits and impact: It supports crew and flight surgeons with early, personalized warnings, and it helps crews manage their own health on long missions where Earth contact is delayed. Tools: React, Tailwind CSS and d3 (JavaScript), with a rule-based statistical engine. It is informed by NASA Human Research Program and NASA OSDR resources. The demo data is synthetic, and ASTRA is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device. Creativity: Instead of one-size-fits-all thresholds, ASTRA works from each astronaut's own baseline and works offline. Factors we considered: data privacy, reliability offline, avoiding alert fatigue, and honest limits on what the data can show.
